title: Dependency Injection
learning_outcomes: Explain what dependency injection contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: constructor injection.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Advanced object design is about collaboration and stable contracts. Interfaces, composition, dependency injection, namespaces, and autoloading help change or test parts independently. In this lesson, focus on constructor injection; then compare it with setter and method injection. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use dependency injection when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Advanced object design is about collaboration and stable contracts. Interfaces, composition, dependency injection, namespaces, and autoloading help change or test parts independently. For dependency injection, begin with constructor injection. Also distinguish setter and method injection; dependencies versus configuration; avoiding hidden dependencies. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: Constructor injection
items.text: Treat the relevant value as untrusted, apply the defense at the correct boundary, and verify a deliberately invalid or hostile-looking input is rejected or encoded.

items.title: Dependencies versus configuration
items.text: Know when to use dependencies versus configuration, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Testing injected collaborators
items.text: Write an assertion about observable behavior and include a boundary or failure case; a passing command alone does not prove the requirement.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Dependency Injection
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$required = ["status", "message"]; $response = ["status" => 200, "message" => "ok"];
echo count(array_intersect($required, array_keys($response))) . " fields matched" . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for dependency injection from top to bottom. Start by identifying constructor injection, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
